title: Henry McKenna's Fairfield sour mash
summary: Irish immigrant Henry McKenna began distilling at Fairfield in Nelson County by 1855 and sold only aged sour mash under his Old Line brand.
bodyMarkdown:
Henry McKenna built one of Nelson County's best-known whiskey names in a very small town. Historian Dixie Hibbs tells his story for the [Kentucky Distillers' Association](https://kybourbon.com/enthusiast-stories/160-years-of-h-mckenna-medicinal-whiskey/). McKenna was a native of County Derry, Ireland. He came to America at 18 and reached Kentucky in 1838, where he worked as a contractor and turnpike builder.

## From mill to still

In 1851 McKenna settled in the village of [Fairfield](https://grokipedia.com/page/fairfield,_kentucky), in Nelson County, and went into milling. Fairfield was first called Turkey Town. It was formally established in 1818 and incorporated in 1870.

By 1855 McKenna was making whisky in a small shed attached to the mill, producing less than a barrel a day. After the Civil War he gave up milling and raised output to a barrel a day. His reputation grew, and in 1883 he built a new brick distillery and added two bonded warehouses, one of stone and one of wood frame.

The bricks were formed from local clay in a wooden mold that made three at a time. The same mold made bricks for his home and for St. Michael's Catholic Church, built on his property nearby. By then the distillery made six barrels a day. McKenna also owned a 360-acre farm, which Hibbs says may have supplied much of his grain.

## One label, made to wait

Unlike many distillers, McKenna made a single product: "H. McKenna Old Line, Hand Made, Sour Mash Whisky." He made no private brands. He never sold whisky to bond until it was three years old, which then counted as old whisky.

It was a family business with Irish roots. His sons Daniel, Stafford and James all took part. Daniel managed the distillery, and James promoted and sold the whisky, opening a Louisville liquor business in 1880. Patrick Sweeney, also from County Derry, was hired as distiller in 1860 and stayed until his death.

McKenna married an Irish wife and returned to Ireland three times. An Irish harp was stenciled under his name on the barrels, and the warehouses eventually held 8,000 barrels.

Physicians across the country wrote letters praising the whisky's purity. Labels for some regions carried the names and towns of these doctors, and advertising called it "Old Whisky for Medicinal Use." McKenna died in 1893.

## Prohibition and after

The distillery made whisky until 1917. After 1919 its barrels went to a Louisville warehouse to be bottled as medicinal whiskey. When Prohibition ended, the plant was repaired, and in 1934 it became the second distillery in Nelson County to resume production. The family sold it to Joseph E. Seagram & Sons in 1941.

## Kentucky today

Hibbs writes that Seagram sold the brand in the early 1980s to [Heaven Hill](https://grokipedia.com/page/Heaven_Hill), the Bardstown company that still makes Henry McKenna bourbon. Heaven Hill itself survived a major fire on November 7, 1996, which destroyed seven warehouses and the distillery but killed no one. Fairfield remains a small town, with 118 residents at the 2020 census. For other early whiskey makers, see [Evan Williams on the Louisville wharf](/stories/evan-williams-on-the-louisville-wharf/) and [Jacob Beam's first barrel](/stories/jacob-beam-sells-old-jakes-first-barrel/).
